svg.aria-label: Diagram: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect flows on Microsoft Entra, showing the authorization code flow from the authorize endpoint through a one-minute authorization code to the token endpoint, which application type uses which flow, what each request parameter defends against, and the rules the platform enforces for browser-based clients including blocking client secrets when an Origin header is present
svg.title: Every parameter in the authorization code flow is a defence against a specific attack
svg.text: Almost every app uses one flow. The parameters are the interesting part.
Each one is a defence against a specific attack, and the platform now enforces several of them rather than recommending them.
The authorization code flow, and the one-minute window in the middle
GET /oauth2/v2.0/authorize
the user signs in, and consents if they have not already
a code comes back — “short lived. Typically, they expire after about 1 minute”
POST /oauth2/v2.0/token
the code is redeemed for an access token
an ID token arrives only with
openid
; a refresh token only with
offline_access
Which flow, by application type — the answer is mostly the same one
Single-page app
auth code + PKCE — “more secure than the implicit flow, which is no longer recommended”
Web app
OIDC to sign in, then auth code to call an API. Confidential: it can hold a secret
Desktop and mobile
auth code. Public client: it cannot hold a secret, whatever the code does
Web API calling onward
on-behalf-of — exchanges the incoming token for an outbound one
Daemon, service, script
client credentials — no user, so no code and no consent screen (post #38)
Each parameter stops one attack
state
cross-site request forgery
nonce
ID token replay
code_challenge
a stolen code being redeemed by
whoever stole it — PKCE
redirect_uri
delivery to an attacker’s address
PKCE is “now recommended for all application types,
both public and confidential clients”, and required
for single-page apps.
Two rules the platform enforces, not advises
“The Microsoft identity platform also prevents the use
of client credentials in all flows in the presence of an
Origin header, to ensure that secrets aren’t used from
within the browser.”
A secret in front-end code is not a lapse the platform
tolerates and warns about. The request simply fails.
And a redirect URI typed
spa
cannot be used by
native or client-credential flows, and one that is not
typed
spa
fails CORS from a browser.
And the consequence nobody plans for
“For refresh tokens sent to a redirect URI registered as spa, the refresh token expires after 24 hours”, and later tokens inherit that
expiry — so a single-page app must “re-run the authorization code flow using an interactive authentication” every day. Users rarely
notice, but it must happen in a top-level frame, because browsers that block third-party cookies will not do it in an iframe.
Microsoft’s own advice about all of the above: these are “low-level protocol details required only when manually crafting and issuing
raw HTTP requests to execute the flow, which we do not recommend”. Use a library; read this to know what it is doing.
Sources: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect protocols, the authorization code flow reference, and Application types, on Microsoft Learn.
